Hook: In 1996 Staples agreed to buy Office Depot, for about four billion dollars. They were two of the three office-supply superstore chains in America. The companies said they competed with everyone who sells a pen: supermarkets, drugstores, warehouse clubs, mail order. Measured that way, their share was small. The Federal Trade Commission answered with the companies' own prices. Where Staples faced no other superstore, it charged more, by about thirteen percent against towns with both rivals, in the comparison as it is usually reported. In June 1997 Judge Thomas Hogan stopped the merger, and the companies abandoned it. It was a case in which the econometrics sat at the centre, and both sides brought economists to argue about it.

The Island has its own version of the case. It has sixty towns. Alder, a chain of office superstores, is in every one; Birch is in some, Cedar in others, and the corner shops are everywhere. Bigger towns, drawn larger, tend to have more chains. Here is Alder's price for a basket of supplies. Where it is alone, it averages 94.78 dollars; where all three chains meet, 85.28. Alder charges about 11 percent more where it has no superstore rival. But look again: towns with Birch alone are cheaper than towns with all three. The towns differ in more than their shops: the big ones have dearer rents. Untangling that is the expert witness's job, and this part follows a merger of Alder and Birch from the first filing to the retrospective, with the truth known.

The question: how is economics used to decide a merger, and what survives cross-examination? What does the law ask, and who has to prove what? Where does a market end? How do economists predict what a merger will do to prices, and to wages? What does a regression look like when the other side's lawyer has it? And, years later, were the predictions right?
Economics, Built. Part fifty-nine: the expert witness.

Part fifty-eight priced a bridge and a bill. This part prices a merger, in front of a judge. By the end you will know what merger law asks and how a case proceeds; how a market is drawn, with the hypothetical monopolist and its traps; how economists predict a merger's effects, from concentration to diversion, pricing pressure, simulation and pass-through; how vertical mergers, cartels, labour markets and regulated prices are analysed; and what a regression looks like under cross-examination, and how retrospectives score the predictions afterwards.
PlayIt: Chapter two. Play it: one market or two?

Your turn. A market, for the law, is a set of products that a single owner could profitably make dearer. The test imagines a hypothetical monopolist of both products in a pair, who raises both prices by five percent. If that pays, the pair is a market; if customers would escape to something else, it is not. You are given two numbers for each pair. The diversion ratio: when one product's price rises, the share of the sales it loses that go to the other. And the other's margin: how much of its price is profit on one more sale. Pair one: Alder and Birch, two superstores. 48 percent of the sales Alder loses go to Birch, and Birch's margin is 13 percent. Pair two: Alder and the corner shops. Only 7 percent of Alder's lost sales go to the shops, whose margin is 15 percent. Pair three: two cement kilns, whose cement is dear to haul far. Only twenty percent of one kiln's lost sales go to the other, but the margin on a tonne is sixty percent. Which pairs are one market?

Here is the arithmetic. When each firm already sets its own price to maximize profit, its margin tells you how fast its sales fall: a five percent rise loses about five percent divided by the margin. The monopolist of both keeps the fraction of those lost sales that go to the partner. Work through the profit, and the rise pays when the diversion ratio exceeds a critical value, X over X plus M, where X is the five percent and M the margin. Alder and Birch: the critical diversion is 27 percent, and the diversion is 48. One market. Alder and the corner shops: 7 percent against a critical 25. Not a market: customers who leave Alder mostly go to another superstore, not to the shops. The kilns: twenty percent against a critical 8. One market, though only a fifth of the lost sales are kept. That surprises people. A high margin means each kept sale is worth a great deal, so even modest diversion makes the rise pay. So, pairs one and three. The superstores' case turned on the first kind of number; the next chapter turns on the third.
Market: The test you just played is the hypothetical-monopolist test, written into the American merger guidelines in 1982. Start with the merging product, imagine one owner of a candidate set, and ask whether a small but significant and non-transitory increase in price, usually five percent, would pay. Here it is in a town with all three chains, with every other price held fixed. A monopolist of Alder alone loses money on any rise: too many customers walk to Birch or Cedar. A monopolist of Alder and Birch gains from a five percent rise. And one of all three superstores gains handsomely. The rule takes the smallest set that passes, so on the Island the market is at most the superstores, not everyone who sells a pen. In the real case Judge Hogan accepted something similar: office supplies sold through office superstores.

Courts often meet the test as critical-loss analysis, introduced by Barry Harris and Joseph Simons in 1989. Before the rise, profit is the margin times sales. After, the margin is bigger but sales fall by a fraction L. The rise pays only if L is below X over X plus M: the critical loss. For the three superstores the margin is 13.4 percent, so the critical loss is 27 percent, and the actual loss from a five percent rise is only 4.9. Defendants long used the formula the other way. Our margins are high, they said, so the critical loss is small; losing only a few customers would sink a price rise; so the market must be broad. Michael Katz and Carl Shapiro, and separately Daniel O'Brien and Abraham Wickelgren, pointed out the catch in 2003. A high margin also tells you that each firm's own customers are hard to lose, or it would have cut its price. High margins mean small actual losses too, unless the customers who leave escape the candidate set altogether. The margin cannot be used for one half of the test and ignored for the other.

The test has a trap, named after a case about cellophane. At competitive prices the three superstores pass easily. Now suppose they already behaved as one firm, with Alder at 100.79 dollars instead of 81.77. Run the same test at those prices, and a further rise does not pay: the monopolist has already raised prices to the point where customers start to leave. So a firm that already has market power looks as if it has none, because at its high price everything looks like a substitute. In 1956 the Supreme Court found that du Pont's cellophane competed with every flexible wrapping, so du Pont had no monopoly. Economists later pointed out that at du Pont's prices that may have been true, and proved nothing. For a merger the test is run at today's prices, which is mostly fine; when the question is whether a firm is already a monopolist, it is not.
Concentration: Once a market is drawn, shares can be counted, and the agencies summarize them with the Herfindahl-Hirschman index: the sum of the squared shares, in percent. In this Island town Alder has 40 percent of superstore sales, Birch 33, Cedar 27. The index is about 3,419. A monopoly scores ten thousand; ten equal firms, a thousand. When Alder and Birch merge, their shares add, and the index rises by twice the product of the two shares: here by about 2,653 points. The index is crude: it knows nothing of who competes with whom inside the market. But it is cheap, and the guidelines turn it into presumptions.

The guidelines draw lines on two numbers: the index after the merger, and its rise. In 1982 a merger was presumed likely to harm competition when the index ended above eighteen hundred and rose by more than a hundred. The 2010 guidelines raised the lines to twenty-five hundred and two hundred, closer to what the agencies were actually challenging. The 2023 guidelines brought them back to eighteen hundred and a hundred, and added the Philadelphia National Bank rule: a merged share above thirty percent, with a rise above a hundred. Here are five proposed Island mergers. Two cement kilns of four, the banks, the hospitals: presumed harmful under every version. The bakeries: under none. And the grocers: presumed in 1982, not in 2010, presumed again in 2023. The economics did not change; the line did. As for the superstores, in every Island town where Alder and Birch meet the index rises by at least 2,611 points, far past any line, because the market of chapter three is so narrow. Draw the market as everyone who sells a pen, and the same merger barely moves the index. That is why the market was the first fight.
Unilateral: Chapter five. Unilateral effects: diversion and pricing pressure.

Concentration is a proxy. The direct question is what the merged firm will want to do with its prices, and the key number is the diversion ratio. When product j's price rises, it loses sales; the diversion ratio to k is the share of those lost sales that k picks up. In this Island town, 48 percent of the customers Alder loses go to Birch, and 52 percent of Birch's go to Alder. Only 7 percent go to the corner shops. Agencies estimate diversion from a demand system when they have one, but also from customer surveys, and from the firms' own records of which rival they lose sales to, which firms keep for their own purposes and must hand over.

Why does the merged firm raise prices, with no agreement with anyone? Part forty-three gave the formula; here is where it comes from. Before the merger Alder sets its price where the profit from one more dollar on every sale just balances the margin lost on customers who leave. After it, some of the customers who leave Alder go to Birch, and Birch's margin on them now belongs to the same owner. One extra term. Rearranged, the extra term acts exactly like a rise in Alder's marginal cost: every sale Alder makes now costs it the Birch sale it might have diverted, worth the diversion ratio times Birch's margin. A higher cost means a higher price. Joseph Farrell and Carl Shapiro called this upward pricing pressure, net of any cost saving from the merger, and its share of the price, the gross upward pricing pressure index, entered the 2010 guidelines as the value of diverted sales. It needs no market definition at all: only a diversion ratio and a margin.

Now the Island's numbers. Alder's GUPPI: 48 percent diversion, times Birch's margin of 10.81 dollars, over Alder's price: 6.3 percent. Birch's is 7.5 percent. The full simulation of Part forty-three, which lets every price adjust, puts Alder's rise at 6 percent and Birch's at 7.2 percent. Cedar's price rises too, by 1.8 percent: no collusion, just dearer competitors. And to hold prices where they are, the merger would have to cut the two chains' marginal costs by 16 to 17 percent, which is a great deal for a shop. In practice the GUPPI is a screen. A value below about five percent is often treated as a weak case; where it is high, the agencies reach for the full model, and the model is where the arguments start.
Simulation: Chapter six. Merger simulation in court.

A simulation needs a demand system, and the demand system must be extended from the prices we see to prices nobody has charged. Take two identical firms. Each sells at a price of one, with a margin of 30 percent and a diversion ratio of 30 percent to the other. Fit four standard demand curves to exactly these numbers. They agree at today's price, in level, slope and diversion. Simulate the merger with each. Linear demand predicts a rise of 6.4 percent; the logit 7.4; demand that falls with the log of price 8.0; and constant elasticity 22.5. The difference is curvature: how the demand curve bends as price rises, which no data at today's prices can reveal. Gregory Werden and his coauthors made the point in 1999, and every simulation presented in court has been attacked along it since. The GUPPI, a first-order number, sits in the middle and does not pretend to know.

So a simulation is attacked in a few standard places. The shape of demand, as you just saw. The elasticities: estimated from which prices, with which instruments, over which years. The conduct: Bertrand competition before the merger is assumed; if the firms were already coordinating, the model is wrong from the start. The outside good: how many buyers would stop buying altogether, which sets how much the inside firms can raise prices together. And the cost savings: left out, or taken on trust. What a simulation adds is not a better number than the evidence it rests on. It is discipline: every assumption is written down, and each can be tested against the documents and the data. Judges have been wary of simulations they could not follow, and readier to credit ones that agree with the firms' own records.

On the Island we can do what no court can: compare a simulation with the truth. Suppose the agency uses a plain logit, calibrated in each town to the prices, the shares and even Alder's true own-price elasticity. Town by town, it predicts the merger will raise Alder's price by 6.9 percent on average. The truth is 11.9. Every town sits above the diagonal, most of all the gold ones, where Cedar is absent and the merger leaves Alder with no superstore rival. The plain logit sends customers who leave Alder to every rival in proportion to its share, so it cannot know that superstores are closer substitutes for each other than for the corner shops. It understates the diversion between the merging chains, and so the harm. Getting the substitution pattern right was the whole point of Part forty-three's random coefficients and nests.
Efficiencies: Chapter seven. Efficiencies, pass-through and entry.

The merging firms always say the deal will save money, and lower costs push prices down. But how much of a saving reaches buyers? That is the pass-through rate. On the Island, cut Alder's marginal cost by two percent with Alder still independent, and its price falls by 67 percent of the saving: the logit's curvature lets the margin absorb the rest. Give the same saving to the merged firm, and it passes on only 53 percent at Alder and about as much at Birch. A lower price at Alder now also steals sales from Birch, which the merged firm owns, so cutting is worth less. That is why the guidelines credit savings only if they are verifiable, specific to the merger, and likely to be passed on, and why the relevant pass-through is the merged firm's, not the industry's.

This was a turning point in the Staples case. The companies projected large savings and said two-thirds of them would be passed on to customers. The FTC's economists and its expert, Orley Ashenfelter, pointed out that a merger's savings are a cost change at one firm, and firms pass on a cost change that hits only them much less than one that hits the whole industry, since rivals' prices do not move with it. They separated the two in Staples' own data, in a regression of this kind: prices on the firm's own costs and on the costs common to everyone. Historically Staples had passed on only about fifteen to seventeen percent of firm-specific cost changes. The judge quoted the comparison in his opinion: two-thirds claimed, fifteen to seventeen percent in the record. The savings could not save the merger.

The other standard defence is entry: if prices rise, someone new will come. On the Island the truth answers it town by town. Where Cedar is already present, the merger raises Alder's price by 5.6 percent: Cedar is the discipline. Where it is not, by 18.9. Across the towns the effect runs from 5 to 22 percent. So the defence's question is whether Cedar would arrive in the towns it has stayed out of, and the guidelines ask that entry be timely, likely and sufficient to undo the harm. A rival that could come is not a rival that is there; a store takes years to open, and Cedar stayed out of those towns for reasons that a merger does not remove.
Vertical: Chapter eight. Vertical mergers: the bargaining model on trial.

So far the merging firms sold the same thing. A vertical merger joins a supplier and its customer. In October 2016 AT&T, which owned the satellite distributor DirecTV, agreed to buy Time Warner, which owned CNN, TNT, HBO and Warner Brothers, for eighty-five billion dollars. The Justice Department sued in 2017. Its theory: once AT&T owned the channels, it could charge rival distributors more for them, and their customers would pay. Its expert, Carl Shapiro, built a bargaining model that predicted bills higher by roughly half a billion dollars a year. In June 2018 Judge Richard Leon let the merger proceed. The model, he wrote, lacked both reliability and factual credibility. The appeals court affirmed in 2019, with a careful distinction: the judge had accepted the bargaining theory as economics, and rejected its prediction on the evidence. The fight was over the inputs.

Here is the model on the Island. A sports channel sells to two distributors: Harbour Cable, with sixty percent of subscribers, and Northern Dish, with forty. The channel and Northern Dish merge. The fee Harbour pays is bargained. Each side's strength is what it would get if talks failed and the channel went dark on Harbour's subscribers. Before the merger, the channel just loses Harbour's fees. After it, some of Harbour's angry subscribers switch to Northern Dish, and their forty dollars a month now belong to the channel's owner. Suppose ten percent would leave and forty-five percent of those would go to Northern Dish. With equal bargaining power, the fee rises by half of that gain: 0.90 dollars a subscriber a month, 45 percent on a two-dollar fee. Rivals' costs rise, and some of that reaches their customers' bills. But there is a saving too. Northern Dish no longer pays a marked-up price for the channel: the elimination of double marginalization of Part forty-four. Spread over all subscribers, rivals' costs rise by 0.54 and the integrated distributor saves 0.80. On these inputs the merger lowers costs on balance.

Now vary the one input nobody can observe directly: how many subscribers would really leave if the channel went dark. The net effect rises with it. Below 14.8 percent, the saving wins; above it, the merger raises costs on balance. In the real trial that number decided a great deal. The government drew it from surveys and industry models. The defence said a long blackout would cost the channels too much in lost fees and advertising to be a credible threat, and Turner offered rival distributors arbitration of fee disputes with no blackout while it ran, which takes the threat off the table. The judge found the government's inputs unconvincing. The lesson for an expert: a model is only as persuasive as the evidence behind its most sensitive input, so find that input first and spend the effort there.
Cartels: Chapter nine. Coordinated effects and cartels.

A merger can also do harm without the merged firm acting alone, by making it easier for the firms that remain to stop competing. Part twelve showed why collusion can sustain itself without any agreement. The guidelines ask whether the merger tips a market towards it. Fewer firms: fewer parties to an understanding, and fewer to watch. Prices everyone can see, so cheating is noticed quickly. Many small, frequent sales, so no single order is worth breaking ranks for. And the maverick: a merger that removes the one firm that kept undercutting the others can do more harm than its share suggests. The step beyond tacit coordination is an explicit cartel, which is a crime.

Cartels are found mostly through leniency: the first member to confess escapes the fine, so cartels tend to betray themselves. Economists add screens, which look for the fingerprints of collusion in prices. Here is fifteen years of the Island's cement price, against its cost. For five of those years the producers ran a cartel. Watch what happens to the price: it sits higher above cost, and it is calmer. Agreeing on every change is costly, so cartels move prices less often and less sharply. A variance screen measures that: the volatility of the month-to-month change in the margin, over a rolling year. During the cartel it falls from about 0.051 to 0.009. The months in the calmest quarter are flagged, in red. A flag is a reason to look, not proof. Rosa Abrantes-Metz and her coauthors built the screen in 2006 from a real case, a bid-rigging ring selling frozen perch to a military supply centre in Philadelphia: when the conspiracy collapsed, the price fell and its standard deviation more than doubled.

Once a cartel is caught, its buyers sue, and the economist's job is the overcharge: how much higher were prices than they would have been? The workhorse is the before-during-after regression: the log price on the log cost and an indicator for the cartel months. The years outside the cartel say how price tracks cost. Here the overcharge is 17.7 percent, against the 18 percent the Island planted. Dividing it out gives the but-for price, what buyers would have paid. The damages are the gap on every tonne bought: about 63 million dollars, and American law trebles them, to give victims a reason to sue and cartels a reason to fear it. Every choice in that regression is contestable: which months count as clean, whether costs were themselves affected, whether the cartel's end was really its end. Part twelve's Dial records how large overcharges usually are; this part adds the Island's.
Witness: Chapter ten. Regression in the witness box.

An economist in court is an expert witness, and a judge decides whether the testimony may be heard at all. In 1993, in Daubert against Merrell Dow, the Supreme Court made the trial judge a gatekeeper: expert testimony must rest on a reliable method, reliably applied. It suggested questions. Can the method be tested, and has it been? Has it been through peer review? What is its error rate? Is it accepted in the field? In 1999 the Kumho Tire case extended the gate to every kind of expert, economists included, and in 2023 the federal rule was amended to say that the judge must find each condition more likely than not. A regression that only its author could defend does not get through.

First, direct examination: the agency's economist presents the price regression, as in Staples. Alder's price rises with town size, because rents do, and bigger towns are also where Birch tends to be. So regress the log of Alder's price on whether Birch and Cedar are present. Without controls, Birch's presence lowers Alder's price by 7.2 percent: the dearer rents of Birch's towns hide part of the effect. Hold costs and size fixed, and the estimate is 10.4 percent, with a standard error under one. The merger's true average effect where both chains are present is 11.9 percent; losing Birch as a rival is close to what the merger does. The agency's witness says: this merger would raise Alder's prices by about ten percent where the two meet.

Now the cross-examination. The other side has the data and the code, and will try every reasonable alternative. Sixteen specifications: costs in or out, size in or out, logs or levels, Cedar in or out. They run from 7.2 to 10.6 percent, and every one is far from zero; the ones that leave out cost and size are lowest, for the reason you saw. Drop any single town, and the estimate stays between 10.2 and 10.8. The best question is a different one: which towns does the average describe? Where Cedar is present, Birch's effect is only 3.8 percent; where it is absent, 15.4. That is a fair point, and an honest witness concedes it and says what it implies: the harm is concentrated in the towns without Cedar, which is where a remedy would have to sell stores. In the real case the FTC's model predicted prices 8.6 percent higher and the defence's 0.9. Ashenfelter and his coauthors later traced the gap to the differences in how the two models were built, and the judge had found the FTC's evidence the more persuasive. The lesson is to put the alternatives on the table yourself, before the other side does.
Labour: Mergers also join employers. Part thirty-eight showed how an employer with few rivals for its workers pays them less than their work is worth. In an Island town, nurses choose between two hospitals and other work, by a logit in the wage. Each hospital pays 32.80 dollars an hour for work worth forty: a markdown of 18 percent, because a hospital that raised its wage would also pay the higher wage to every nurse it already has. The hospitals merge. Wages fall to 30.26, by 7.7 percent, and the markdown widens to 24. It is the diversion argument again, on the other side of the market: a nurse who quits one hospital for the other no longer leaves the employer. No patient's price need change at all. A review that looks only at what buyers pay would miss this harm entirely.

Is it real? Elena Prager and Matt Schmitt studied American hospital mergers. After the quarter of mergers that raised employer concentration most, wage growth slowed by about 1.7 percentage points a year for nurses and pharmacy workers, and 1.1 for other skilled workers, whose skills are worth most in hospitals; for unskilled workers, who can work anywhere, they found no effect. Employers can also simply agree not to compete for workers. Alan Krueger and Orley Ashenfelter read the 2016 franchise contracts of America's big chains and found that 58 percent barred one franchisee from hiring another's workers. After their paper circulated, state attorneys general pressed many chains to drop the clauses, and the federal agencies had already warned that naked no-poach agreements could be prosecuted as crimes. In 2023 the merger guidelines gave labour markets a guideline of their own. The tools are the same as for buyers: a market, shares, diversion, now measured in workers who would switch employers.
Retro: Suppose the Island's court let the merger through. A year later, an economist at the agency runs a retrospective. In the towns where Alder and Birch met, prices after the merger are compared with prices before; in the towns where they did not meet, the same, to remove whatever else changed. The difference in differences: the merger raised Alder's price by 11.7 percent, close to the truth of 11.9. Now set the predictions against it. The GUPPI screen said 9.0. The agency's plain-logit simulation said 6.9, too low, for the reason of chapter six. That is the real value of a retrospective: it scores the tools, so that the next prediction is made with a better one.

Real retrospectives have become a literature of their own. Orley Ashenfelter and Daniel Hosken studied five consumer-product mergers that the agencies had let through, near the line where they might have been challenged. Four raised prices, typically by three to seven percent. Zack Cooper and his coauthors found that mergers between hospitals within five miles of each other were followed by prices about six percent higher. And a 2024 study counted only thirteen hospital mergers challenged by the Federal Trade Commission between 2000 and 2020, about one percent of them, when the agency's own standard screens would have flagged about a fifth. These samples are selected, by data and by interest, and averaging across them is risky; Part forty-four's Dial records the disagreement. Read together, they suggest that American review has let through more harmful mergers than it has blocked harmless ones, though that conclusion is itself disputed.
Regulated: Some markets have room for one firm only: one water main, one power grid. There the economics of merger review gives way to regulation, and economists testify in rate cases. The classic method is cost of service. The Island's water company may recover its operating costs, depreciation and taxes, plus an allowed return on the capital it has invested, its rate base: seven percent of 500. The total is the revenue requirement, 105, and the price is that divided by the volume sold. The hearings are about the allowed return, which American courts since the Hope Natural Gas case of 1944 have said must be commensurate with returns on investments of corresponding risk, and about whether each investment was prudent. Part ten showed the catch: if the allowed return beats the cost of capital, the firm uses too much capital; and since every saving is passed straight to customers at the next case, the firm has little reason to look for one.

In 1983 Stephen Littlechild proposed a different deal for Britain's soon-to-be-privatized telephone company: cap the price, not the profit. The price may rise each year by inflation minus X, a number the regulator sets for five years at a time. Between resets, whatever the firm saves it keeps, so it has every reason to save. On the Island, assume that under the cap the water company's costs fall four percent a year in real terms, against one percent under cost of service. The capped price falls in real terms, and the firm's margin grows as its costs fall faster. At each reset the regulator brings the price down to cost, and customers collect the savings, later rather than sooner. After fifteen years the real price is 0.54 under the cap against 0.86 under cost of service. The numbers hang on the effort each regime is assumed to induce, which is the part a regulator has to estimate, and the next X is argued over by economists on both sides, as rate cases were.

One more regulated price: access. The Island's telephone company owns the network, which costs 3 dollars a customer, and a retail service costing 2; customers pay 10. A rival wants to rent the network and sell its own service. What should it pay? The efficient component pricing rule, associated with William Baumol and Robert Willig, says: the network's cost plus the margin the incumbent loses on each customer it gives up, 8 dollars. Then the entrant profits only if its retail service costs less than 2, so only more efficient rivals enter. The objection is plain: the rule hands the incumbent its monopoly margin on every customer it loses, and competition never touches it. Many regulators price access at cost instead, and accept less efficient entrants as the price of competition. Which rule is right depends on whether the retail margin is a reward for something, or just a monopoly's rent.
Dials: Chapter fourteen. The Dials: pass-through and cartel overcharges.

This part opens one Dial and returns to another. The new one is the pass-through of a merger's cost savings. Staples' own history: about 15 to 17 percent of firm-specific cost changes reached its prices, the number the court set against the companies' two-thirds. The Island's Alder, alone, passes on 67 percent of a saving; merged with Birch, 53. The status: it depends on the setting, on the curvature of demand and on how many of the firm's rivals share the saving. But the direction holds everywhere: a saving one firm enjoys alone is passed on less than one that the whole industry shares, and a merged firm passes on less than an independent one.

The second Dial is Part twelve's: how much cartels overcharge. John Connor's collection of hundreds of published estimates has a median of about 23 percent. Marcel Boyer and Rachidi Kotchoni, correcting the same collection for the ways estimates are made and published, put the median at about 16. The lysine cartel of the 1990s, about 20. And the Island's cement cartel, measured by this part's regression: 17.7, against eighteen planted. The status stays contested. The low end and the high end imply very different fines, and whether the published estimates are biased upward is itself the argument.
